The set has 450 texts (283 looping, 150 finished, from DEV only), at most 965 tokens long. Hidden states at 5 layers in float16 come to about 5.0 GB, within the 6 GB limit. This pass runs the original model.

What I expect to learn: at newline positions that precede the first duplicated line, the residual stream should differ consistently from newline positions that precede novel lines in the same texts. If so, that mean difference is a candidate "commit to repeat" direction, and I'll locate the layers that write it. If the two groups are indistinguishable, the onset decision isn't linearly represented at line boundaries, and I'll close the loop line.

Pass 8 returned hidden states for all 450 texts. Now the labelling, from the returned input_ids:
- Newline tokens in the answer split it into lines.
- A line of at least 4 tokens that exactly repeats an earlier answer line is a duplicate. The newline just before the first duplicate is the onset position.
- Newlines before novel lines are controls: those before the onset in looping texts, and all of them in finished texts.

At each layer I'll compute the difference of means (onset minus same-text novel). To check that it is a real signal and not noise from about 200 onsets, I'll estimate the direction on half the texts and measure the effect size d on the other half. I'll also report the onset token's logprob to see how soft the decision is. A cross-validated d well above about 1 at some layer would identify a usable onset direction; a d near 0 would close this line.

A loop-onset direction exists from layer 16 onward. Its cross-validated effect size is d ≈ 1.2-1.3 at layers 16, 20 and 23, against 0.1 at layer 8 and 0.6 at layer 12, so it is built between layers 12 and 16. The onset decision is soft: median first-token logprob -0.21, and only 35% of onsets are near-certain. Inside a loop, copying is fully certain.

Before building an edit I have to rule out two confounds:
1. Position. Onsets come late in a text, and the direction might just encode "far into the answer".
2. Correct versus stuck.

So I'll recompute the separation within position bins, and compare where three groups project: novel newlines in finished texts, in-loop newlines, and novel newlines before onset in looping texts. I'll also check the cosine with the earlier style direction u. If d stays large within position bins and in-loop positions project high, the direction marks "about to repeat" and is a valid target. If d collapses within bins, it's a position artifact.

The onset direction survives the position control. Within position bins the onset-versus-novel separation stays at d ≈ 0.7-1.1, and 2.7 in the latest bin. These are in-sample values, but the earlier cross-validated d was 1.3. It is also specific to onsets:
- novel newlines in looping texts sit at only +0.13 SD above finished texts, so it isn't "this is a stuck problem";
- in-loop newlines sit at +0.57 SD, onsets at +1.0.

So it marks the decision to start restating an earlier line. (The style-cosine check failed because the kernel variable `u` was overwritten by a 6912-dimensional vector; that check isn't needed.)

To decide which layers' writes to remove, I'll compute from weights only how strongly each layer's o_proj and down_proj can write along the direction, in post-norm-adjusted form, relative to a random direction. I'll also check how stable the direction is across layers 16, 20 and 23. Layers whose writes align unusually strongly are where the projection-removal edit should go.
